opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the starting point is that AI has never really had its own language. Lisp and Prolog were attempts, and they were great for symbolic AI, but they didn't scale and they didn't support learning. Then deep learning came along and we ended up doing everything in Python, with libraries like PyTorch and JAX bolted on. Python was never designed for AI. It's a hack that happened to win. You have automatic differentiation and GPU support as afterthoughts in a library, and if you want reasoning, knowledge representation, or anything symbolic, you're on your own.

TensorLogic comes from an observation that I think is surprisingly deep: a logical rule and a tensor equation are essentially the same thing. Take a Datalog rule like "x is the grandparent of z if x is a parent of y and y is a parent of z." If you represent the relations as Boolean tensors, that rule is an Einstein summation. You join on y, you project y out, and then you apply a step function. The join is the tensor product and the projection is the summation. Once you see that, you realize the whole of logic programming and the whole of neural networks can be written in a single construct, the tensor equation.

So the language is extremely simple. There's basically one kind of statement. But with that one statement you can write a transformer in a dozen or so lines. You can write a graph neural network, a kernel machine, or a probabilistic graphical model, and you can write symbolic rules. You can mix them freely, because they're all the same kind of object.

What I find most exciting is what happens when you move from Boolean tensors to real-valued ones and embed the objects. Then you get reasoning in embedding space. There's a temperature parameter. At zero temperature you get purely deductive reasoning, with no hallucinations. The conclusions follow from the rules. As you raise the temperature you get analogical, similarity-based reasoning, which is what makes neural networks generalize. So you have a dial between the reliability of logic and the flexibility of deep learning, instead of having to pick one.

As for suitability, I'd say it's suitable in the way a good language for a field should be. It captures the fundamental operations of the field directly, so you're not fighting the language. Learning is just gradient descent on the tensors, and the tensors can be anything. Inference is forward chaining or backward chaining, which are the same as forward and backward propagation in a different guise. Transparency comes almost for free, because you can read off the rules.

Now, I'm not going to pretend it's done. A language lives or dies by its ecosystem: tooling, compilers, efficient sparse implementations, people actually using it. Python won on ecosystem, not on design. So the real test is whether people pick it up and find that problems that were painful become easy. But my bet is that the field needs something like this. If you think the future of AI is unifying learning and reasoning, which I do, then you want a language where that unification is the native thing and not glue code. TensorLogic is my proposal for what that language looks like.

r001.rationale: The response says TensorLogic directly captures AI operations, but does not compare task-appropriate abstraction with universality.

r002.rationale: It calls Python an unsuitable, accidental choice for AI, but does not explain that familiarity with a language leads people to use it for such tasks.

r003.rationale: It equates logical rules with tensor equations and describes their operations, but does not predict that users will conceptualize programs as tensor operations rather than logic.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the way I think about it is that every programming language is really a bet on what the fundamental operations of computation should be. Lisp bet on list manipulation and recursion, Prolog bet on logical inference, and Python, for all its popularity in AI, is just a general-purpose scripting language that happens to have good libraries bolted onto it. None of them were designed for what AI actually is, which is this marriage of reasoning and learning.

Tensor Logic comes from a very simple observation that I think people keep missing. A logical rule, a Datalog rule, say, and an Einstein summation over tensors are the same thing. If you write a rule like "grandparent of X and Z if parent of X and Y and parent of Y and Z," that is literally a join followed by a projection, and a join followed by a projection is exactly what an einsum does. The indices that appear in the body but not the head get summed out. So once you see that, you realize you can have one construct, the tensor equation, and get logic as a special case when the tensors are Boolean, and get neural networks as a special case when they are real-valued and you throw a nonlinearity on the end.

So why do I think it is suitable as a language for AI, as opposed to just a neat trick? A few reasons. First, it is tiny. The whole language is essentially one thing. That is what you want from a foundation, the way the lambda calculus or first-order logic is tiny. Second, it gives you both halves of AI natively. You can do deep learning in it, you can write a transformer in a dozen lines, but you can also do symbolic reasoning in it, and crucially, you can do them in the same representation, so you do not have this painful boundary where you are shipping tensors over to a symbolic engine and back. Third, and this is the part I care most about, it lets you reason in embedding space in a way that is sound. You can turn a knob, essentially a temperature, and at zero you get crisp deductive logic with no hallucination, because the system can only derive what follows from the rules, and as you raise it you get analogical, similarity-based reasoning that neural networks are good at. That continuum is, to me, the key to getting the reliability of symbolic systems and the flexibility of neural ones at once.

Now, I want to be careful about the word "language." It is not meant to replace Python as the thing you write your web server in. It is meant to be the thing that PyTorch and Prolog and probabilistic programming languages are all approximations of. Whether it ends up being the surface syntax people type, or more of an intermediate representation that compilers and other languages target, I think is an open question and honestly I am fine either way. The important claim is not about syntax, it is that there is a single mathematical object underneath all of these AI paradigms, and once you expose it, a lot of things that currently take whole frameworks become one-liners.

Where I think the real test will come is in the tooling and the ecosystem. A language lives or dies on its compilers, its debuggers, its libraries, and on whether it is fast on GPUs, and a lot of that is still being built. But the conceptual argument I am very confident in. We have been trying to unify learning and reasoning for decades, and I think the reason it has been hard is that we kept trying to glue two different things together, instead of noticing that they were already the same thing.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts TensorLogic’s AI focus with Python’s general-purpose role, but does not state that matching abstraction level to the task matters more than universality.

r002.rationale: It says Python is popular in AI and has libraries added to it, but does not explain that familiarity leads people to choose languages for tasks they suit poorly.

r003.rationale: It describes tensor equations as a unified construct for logic and neural networks, but does not predict that users will think in tensor operations instead of logical operations.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether it gives you the right abstractions. In AI, you want to learn from data, but you also want to express knowledge, impose constraints, and reason about things. Today, those often live in separate systems.

The appeal of TensorLogic is to bring tensor computation and logic into the same language. Tensors give you a natural way to express neural computation, while logic gives you a natural way to express relationships and rules. Ideally, you could combine those without constantly translating between two different worlds.

But a unifying language has to earn its keep. Can you express useful models simply? Can you execute them efficiently? Can you understand why your program isn’t doing what you intended? That’s what would make it suitable as a programming language for AI—not just having an elegant connection between the mathematics.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether TensorLogic provides the right abstractions, but does not compare task-appropriate abstraction with universality.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss familiarity with a language causing people to use it for poorly suited tasks.

r003.rationale: It describes tensors and logic as useful for different purposes, but does not predict that users will think in tensor operations rather than logical operations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: what are the abstractions you want in a programming language for AI? If you’re doing deep learning, you want tensors and operations on tensors. If you’re doing symbolic reasoning, you want predicates, variables, and rules. And ideally, you shouldn’t have to choose between those two worlds.

The idea behind TensorLogic is that they can share a common language. You can view a relation as a Boolean tensor, for example, and express logical operations through tensor operations. That gives you a way to bring learning and reasoning together, rather than building two separate systems and then trying to connect them.

But a common representation is only part of the challenge. The language also needs to make it easy to express what you want, and the compiler needs to execute it efficiently. A logical relation might be enormous but very sparse; you don’t want to materialize a gigantic tensor just because that’s the mathematical representation.

So I see it as a promising foundation for an AI programming language. The ambition is to let you specify knowledge where you have knowledge, learn where you have data, and combine the two within the same program.

r001.rationale: It asks which abstractions suit AI tasks and says learning and reasoning should share a language, but does not say task-appropriate abstraction matters more than universality.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss familiarity with a language leading people to use it for tasks it is poorly suited to.

r003.rationale: It says logical operations can be expressed through tensor operations, but does not predict that users will think of their programs in terms of tensor operations rather than logic.
